input:
Start-up

Before the plate heat exchanger is started up, it is essential to carry out a thorough check of the unit in order to ensure that everything is in order. The plate pack should be confirmed as properly closed, with the bolts tightened evenly in the correct sequence and all gaskets correctly seated in their grooves. The vents at the high points of both circuits should then be opened, and the cold circuit should be filled first and vented until liquid flows steadily from the vent, after which the hot circuit can be filled and vented in the same way. It is important to note that an exchanger started with air still trapped inside the pack will typically exhibit uneven flow distribution and misleading temperature readings, so venting should never be rushed. The whole unit should also be checked carefully for leaks while the circuits are full and still cold, as it is much easier to correct a gasket leak at this stage than after heating has begun. The flows should then be started at a low rate and increased gradually to the operating rate, and the hot circuit should be brought up to temperature slowly, in order to avoid thermal shock to the plates and gaskets. During this period, the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressure drop across the pack should be monitored closely. Start-up can be regarded as complete when both flows have reached their operating rates, the outlet temperatures are stable and no leaks are present.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the flows should be maintained at the rates required by the duty, and the inlet and outlet temperatures and pressures should be read and recorded on every round. Keeping a proper record is extremely valuable, because fouling of the plates usually develops gradually and reveals itself as a slow drift in the readings: the outlet temperature of the heated stream falls below its earlier value at unchanged flows, while the pressure drop across the pack rises. Operators should also ensure that the strainers in both inlet lines are kept clean, since a blocked strainer can starve the exchanger and produce symptoms similar to fouling. Care should be taken not to run the exchanger with one circuit stopped while the other remains hot, as the stagnant fluid may boil locally or deposit solids on the plates. The pressures within both circuits should be kept within the rated limits of the plates and gaskets, and any weeping at a gasket should be reported as a defect rather than accepted as normal. Where the temperature of the heated stream must be controlled within a band, adjustments should be made to the hot-side flow and sufficient time allowed for the unit to settle before further adjustments are made, in order to avoid hunting.

Alarms

The unit is provided with alarms that warn the operator of abnormal conditions. A high differential pressure across the plate pack indicates that the flow passages have become obstructed, for example by fouling of the plates or by solids carried into the pack. In this event, the throughput should be reduced and the differential pressure observed: if it falls and remains stable, operation may continue at the reduced rate and the condition should be reported. However, if the differential pressure remains high, the exchanger should be taken out of service following the shutdown procedure and the plates should be cleaned before the unit is returned to duty, as forcing the exchanger to operate against a rising differential pressure can damage the gaskets and may lead to a leak between the two circuits.

A low flow alarm in either circuit indicates that the supply to that circuit has failed, which may be due to a stopped pump, a closed valve or a blocked strainer. The operator should check the running of the pump, the position of the valves and the condition of the strainer, in that order. The other circuit should not be left running hot against a circuit that is stagnant. If the flow cannot be restored promptly, the unit should be shut down following the shutdown procedure and the fault reported. The alarm can be regarded as cleared only when the flow has been re-established and the temperatures have returned to their normal operating values.

Shutdown

When the exchanger is to be shut down, the flows should be reduced gradually and the hot circuit should be stopped first, so that the pack can cool under flow in the cold circuit and no hot fluid is left standing in the plates. The cold flow should be continued until the outlet temperatures have fallen close to the cold inlet temperature, after which the cold circuit can also be stopped. The inlet and outlet valves of both circuits should then be closed, the vents opened and both circuits drained completely. It should be noted that an exchanger left standing full of process fluid will foul while it stands, and a circuit left full in freezing weather may be damaged by ice formation. Where the fluids concerned are known to foul or set when cold, the plates should be cleaned before any extended standstill and the unit left drained, vented and open to inspection. Finally, any gasket weeping, plate damage and the general condition of the pack found during draining should be reported, so that the next start-up can begin from a known state.
target:
Start-up

Confirm before start-up that the plate pack is closed, that the bolts are tightened evenly in the sequence the frame marking shows, and that every gasket sits in its groove. Open the vents at the high points of both circuits. Fill the cold circuit first and vent it until liquid flows steadily from the vent; then fill and vent the hot circuit in the same way. An exchanger started with air trapped in the pack gives uneven flow and false temperature readings, and the venting step is not complete until both circuits run free of air. Check the whole unit for leaks while the circuits are full and still cold: a gasket leak found at this stage is corrected by re-tightening or by replacing the gasket, and no leak is acceptable once heating begins. Start the flows at a low rate and raise them gradually to the operating rate. Bring the hot circuit up to temperature slowly: a sudden admission of hot fluid shocks the plates and the gaskets and can start a leak at a joint that was sound when cold. Watch the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressure drop across the pack as the unit comes up to duty. Open each drain briefly before filling and confirm that it runs clear, so that debris left in the lines by maintenance is found at the drain and not in the plate pack. Start-up is complete when both flows are at their operating rates, the outlet temperatures are steady, and no joint leaks.

Normal operation

Hold the flows at the rates the duty requires and read the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressures at the unit on every round. Record the readings: the record, not a single reading, shows the state of the exchanger, because fouling announces itself as a slow drift — the outlet temperature of the heated stream falls away from its earlier value at unchanged flows, and the pressure drop across the pack rises. Keep the strainers in both inlet lines clean: a blocked strainer starves the exchanger and mimics fouling at the pressure gauges. Do not run the exchanger with one circuit stopped while the other is hot: a stagnant circuit boils locally or deposits solids on the plates, and the damage is done before the temperatures show it. Keep both circuits within the pressure the plates and gaskets are rated for, and treat any weep at a gasket as a defect to be reported, not as a normal feature of the unit. Where the heated stream must stay within a temperature band, adjust the hot-side flow and re-read the outlet temperature after the adjustment has had time to settle; repeated adjustment before the unit settles produces hunting and teaches the record nothing. Compare each round's readings with the record of the rounds before it: a change that appears between one round and the next is an event and is reported at once, while a change that grows slowly over many rounds is fouling or a failing component, and the two conditions are handled differently.

Alarms

The unit raises two alarms. Each alarm names the condition it detects, and the operator action for each alarm is stated with it.

A high differential pressure across the plate pack means the flow passages are obstructed, by fouling on the plates or by solids carried into the pack. Reduce the throughput and watch the differential pressure: if it falls and holds, continue at the reduced rate and report the condition. If the differential pressure stays high, take the exchanger out of service under the shutdown procedure and clean the plates before the unit is returned to duty; an exchanger forced to run against a rising differential pressure damages its gaskets and can open a leak between the circuits.

A low flow in either circuit means the supply to that circuit has failed: a stopped pump, a closed valve or a blocked strainer. Check the running of the pump, the position of the valves and the state of the strainer, in that order. Do not leave the other circuit running hot against a stagnant one. If flow cannot be restored promptly, shut the unit down under the shutdown procedure and report the fault; the alarm is cleared only when flow is re-established and the temperatures have returned to their operating values.

Shutdown

Reduce the flows gradually and stop the hot circuit first, so that the pack cools under flow in the cold circuit and no part of the plates is left holding hot stagnant fluid. Continue the cold flow until the outlet temperatures have fallen close to the cold inlet temperature, then stop the cold circuit. Close the inlet and outlet valves of both circuits, open the vents, and drain both circuits completely. An exchanger left standing full of process fluid fouls while it stands, and a circuit left full in freezing weather can be damaged by the ice that forms in it. Where the fluids foul or set when cold, clean the plates before a long standstill and leave the unit drained, vented and open to inspection. Report any gasket weep, any damaged plate and the state of the pack found at draining, so that the next start-up begins from a known condition. Tag the isolated valves, and enter the shutdown in the unit log with the readings taken at the moment of stopping, so that the condition in which the exchanger was left stands on record for the crew that returns it to service.
